nationality_or_literary_tradition: Mvskoke (Muscogee) Nation; poet, musician and playwright writing in English
literary_identity: Mvskoke poet and saxophonist, US Poet Laureate 2019-22, whose work fused the Native American Renaissance with jazz and who was the first Native American to hold the laureateship
biography: Joy Harjo was born on 9 May 1951 in Tulsa, Oklahoma, and is an enrolled member of the Mvskoke (Creek) Nation; her father was Muscogee and her mother of Cherokee, French and Irish descent. She studied at the Institute of American Indian Arts in Santa Fe, took a BA from the University of New Mexico and an MFA from the Iowa Writers' Workshop, and taught for many years at the University of New Mexico and the University of Illinois. The Last Song (1975) and What Moon Drove Me to This? (1979) preceded She Had Some Horses (Thunder's Mouth Press, 1983), the book that made her name. Secrets from the Center of the World (1989), In Mad Love and War (Wesleyan, 1990) - which won the American Book Award - The Woman Who Fell from the Sky (Norton, 1994) and A Map to the Next World (2000) followed, along with the memoir Crazy Brave (2012) and the poetry collections Conflict Resolution for Holy Beings (2015) and An American Sunrise (2019). She performs with her band the Arrow Dynamics, has released several albums of music with her saxophone and voice, and was named US Poet Laureate in 2019, serving three terms to 2022; she edited the Norton Anthology of Native Nations Poetry, When the Light of the World Was Subdued, Our Songs Came Through (2020).
literary_profile: The Last Song (1975); What Moon Drove Me to This? (1979); She Had Some Horses (1983); Secrets from the Center of the World (1989); In Mad Love and War (1990); The Woman Who Fell from the Sky (1994); A Map to the Next World (2000); How We Became Human: New and Selected Poems (2004); She Had Some Horses (reissued 2008); Crazy Brave (2012); Conflict Resolution for Holy Beings (2015); and An American Sunrise (2019).
stylistic_characteristics: Free verse that moves by association and repetition rather than by argument; a syntax of invocation; the line broken where breath breaks; animals, weather and the Oklahoma landscape as agents rather than scenery; and the rhythm of blues and jazz carried into the poem.
intellectual_concerns: Indigenous survival, removal and return; the Mvskoke homeland and the Trail of Tears; women's lives and violence against women; the natural world as a network of persons; music and ceremony as forms of memory; and the crossing of the American present with a mythic one.
historical_significance: Harjo is the best-known Native American poet of her generation and the first Native American US Poet Laureate; She Had Some Horses is a central text of the Native American Renaissance and of the poetry of the 1980s, and the Norton's four selections are drawn from four different decades of her work, which makes her the anthology's fullest representation of a Native poet.

birthplace: Wellpinit, Spokane Indian Reservation, Washington, United States
nationality_or_literary_tradition: Spokane and Coeur d'Alene; poet, novelist and filmmaker writing in English
literary_identity: Spokane writer whose first books made him the most widely read Native American author of his generation and whose work moved between lyric, satire, film and young-adult fiction
biography: Sherman Joseph Alexie Jr. was born on 7 October 1966 on the Spokane Indian Reservation at Wellpinit, Washington, the son of a Spokane father and a Coeur d'Alene mother, and grew up in poverty; he was hydrocephalic as an infant, suffered seizures, and read voraciously, leaving the reservation school for Reardan High School where he was the only Indian student. He took a BA from Washington State University, where he studied with Alex Kuo, and published The Business of Fancydancing (Hanging Loose Press, 1992) at twenty-five; it mixes poems and short stories and was followed by the story collection The Lone Ranger and Tonto Fistfight in Heaven (1993), which won the PEN/Hemingway Award, and the novel Reservation Blues (1995). Indian Killer (1996) was a thriller, and The Summer of Black Widows (1996) gathered his poems. He wrote the screenplay for Smoke Signals (1998), the first feature film written, directed and acted by Native Americans to reach wide release, and directed The Business of Fancydancing as a film in 2002. The Absolutely True Diary of a Part-Time Indian (2007) won the National Book Award for Young People's Literature; later books include Blasphemy: New and Selected Stories (2012) and You Don't Have to Say You Love Me (2017), a memoir about his mother. He has spoken publicly about depression and about having been sexually abused as a child, and in 2018 faced allegations of sexual harassment, which he has denied.
literary_profile: The Business of Fancydancing (1992); The Lone Ranger and Tonto Fistfight in Heaven (1993); Reservation Blues (1995); Indian Killer (1996); The Summer of Black Widows (1996); The Toughest Indian in the World (2000); Ten Little Indians (2003); The Absolutely True Diary of a Part-Time Indian (2007); Blasphemy (2012); and You Don't Have to Say You Love Me (2017).
stylistic_characteristics: A demotic, joke-telling free verse and prose poem built on the one-liner; abrupt turns from comedy to grief; reservation speech with its own timing; and a habit of naming brands, basketball players and television shows as the common culture of his characters.
intellectual_concerns: Reservation life, poverty and endurance; basketball as an image of both escape and entrapment; alcoholism and its inheritance; the commodification of Indian identity for tourists and readers; and the grief of a family and a people, handled through comedy.
historical_significance: Alexie was for two decades the most widely taught Native American writer in American schools, and the Norton's four selections - three poems from the 1990s and a story - represent both the lyric and the fictional sides of his early work. 'This Is What It Means to Say Phoenix, Arizona' is the story from which Smoke Signals was developed. The harassment allegations of 2018 have changed how his work is taught without removing it from the anthologies.
bibliographical_notes: The book list, the 1993 PEN/Hemingway Award, the 2007 National Book Award and the film credits are from the Wikipedia article checked against the Poetry Foundation author page; the allegations of 2018 are mentioned without detail and are not part of any work record.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: African American; poet and essayist writing in English
literary_identity: African American poet, US Poet Laureate 1993-95 and Pulitzer Prize winner 1987, whose sequence Thomas and Beulah recovered her grandparents' lives in a form both lyric and historical
biography: Rita Frances Dove was born on 28 August 1952 in Akron, Ohio, and grew up there as the daughter of the first Black chemist at the Goodyear Tire & Rubber Company. She was a Presidential Scholar in 1970, graduated summa cum laude from Miami University of Ohio, studied at the Universität Tübingen on a Fulbright and took an MFA from the Iowa Writers' Workshop in 1977. The Yellow House on the Corner (Carnegie Mellon, 1980) and Museum (1983) came first, and Thomas and Beulah (1986) - a sequence about her maternal grandparents' migration from the South to Akron - won the Pulitzer Prize in 1987. She published Grace Notes (1989), the novel Through the Ivory Gate (1992), Mother Love (1995), a reworking of the Demeter-Persephone myth, and On the Bus with Rosa Parks (1999). She was US Poet Laureate from 1993 to 1995, the youngest ever appointed, and served as Poet Laureate of Virginia from 2004 to 2006; her later work includes American Smooth (2004), Sonata Mulattica (2009), a book-length sequence on the Black violinist George Bridgetower, and Playlist for the Apocalypse (2021). She has edited The Best American Poetry (2000) and The Penguin Anthology of Twentieth-Century American Poetry (2011), and teaches at the University of Virginia.
literary_profile: The Yellow House on the Corner (1980); Museum (1983); Thomas and Beulah (1986); Grace Notes (1989); Through the Ivory Gate (1992); Mother Love (1995); On the Bus with Rosa Parks (1999); American Smooth (2004); Sonata Mulattica (2009); and Playlist for the Apocalypse (2021).
stylistic_characteristics: Formal control inside free verse; short lyrics arranged into sequences with a narrative arc; a diction that moves between the plain and the archaic without strain; persona poems in the voices of historical figures; and a strong sense of the poem as a shaped object with a turn and a close.
intellectual_concerns: The Great Migration and the lives of ordinary Black Americans in the industrial Midwest; family history and inheritance; music, dance and the performing body; the classical and mythological past in relation to Black experience; and the pressures of history on a private life.
historical_significance: Dove was the youngest US Poet Laureate and the second African American to hold the post, and Thomas and Beulah is one of the most admired American sequences of the 1980s, a model for the book-length historical lyric. The Norton prints ten of her selections - three Adolescence poems, three sections of Thomas and Beulah and four other lyrics - which is more than any other poet in the anthology's period.
bibliographical_notes: The collection list, the 1987 Pulitzer, the laureateship dates and the editorships are from the Wikipedia article checked against the Poetry Foundation author page; the contents of The Yellow House on the Corner and Thomas and Beulah were checked against their tables of contents.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Chinese American; novelist and short-story writer writing in English
literary_identity: Chinese American novelist whose The Joy Luck Club, built from sixteen interlinked stories, was the first book by an Asian American writer to reach the top of the New York Times bestseller list
biography: Amy Ruth Tan was born on 19 February 1952 in Oakland, California, to Chinese immigrant parents: her father John, an electrical engineer and Baptist minister who had left China in 1949, and her mother Daisy, who had left a first husband and three daughters in Shanghai. The family moved repeatedly before settling in Santa Clara, and Tan grew up between the English of school and the Chinese of home. Her father and elder brother both died of brain tumours within months of each other when she was fifteen. She took a BA and an MA in linguistics at San Jose State University and began a doctorate at the University of California, Berkeley, which she abandoned for business writing. The Joy Luck Club (G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1989) grew out of a story written for a writers' workshop and became a bestseller and a film in 1993. The Kitchen God's Wife (1991), The Hundred Secret Senses (1995), The Bonesetter's Daughter (2001) and Saving Fish from Drowning (2005) followed, along with the memoir The Opposite of Fate (2003) and, after a long silence following a neurological illness, Where the Past Begins (2017). She has also written two children's books.
literary_profile: The Joy Luck Club (1989); The Kitchen God's Wife (1991); The Hundred Secret Senses (1995); The Bonesetter's Daughter (2001); Saving Fish from Drowning (2005); The Opposite of Fate: A Book of Musings (2003); and Where the Past Begins: A Writer's Memoir (2017).
stylistic_characteristics: Plain first-person narration in alternating voices; a structure of interlinked stories rather than a single plot; Chinese words and sayings left untranslated in the mothers' speech; and a syntax that keeps the rhythm of oral storytelling.
intellectual_concerns: Mothers and daughters across a language and a history; the Chinese Civil War, the Japanese invasion and emigration to America; the pressure of the model-minority expectation; and the work of recovering a mother's past that a daughter has not been told.
historical_significance: The Joy Luck Club sold millions of copies, was translated widely and was filmed by Wayne Wang in 1993, and it made the Chinese American immigrant family a mainstream subject of American fiction; 'Two Kinds' - the chapter the Norton prints - is one of the most anthologised pieces of Asian American writing and is a standard text in courses on the immigrant bildungsroman.
bibliographical_notes: The novels, the dates and the family biography are from the Wikipedia article checked against the Poetry Foundation author page and the Putnam first edition's author note; the children's books are counted without individual titles.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Mexican American (Chicana); novelist, short-story writer and poet writing in English
literary_identity: Chicana writer whose The House on Mango Street made the Mexican American girl's voice a fixture of the American canon and sold millions of copies outside the classroom
biography: Sandra Cisneros was born on 20 December 1954 in Chicago, the only daughter among seven children of a Mexican father and a Mexican American mother, and the family moved constantly between Chicago and Mexico City. She took a BA from Loyola University Chicago and an MFA from the Iowa Writers' Workshop, where she felt her Chicago neighbourhood was not considered a proper subject for literature. Bad Boys (1980) was a chapbook; The House on Mango Street (Arte Público Press, 1984) grew out of that Iowa experience, and after Random House picked it up in 1991 it sold more than six million copies. Woman Hollering Creek and Other Stories (Random House, 1991) established her as a short-story writer. Since then she has published Loose Woman (1994) and other poetry, the novel Caramelo (2002), the memoir A House of My Own (2015), and she was awarded the PEN/Nabokov Award and the National Medal of Arts; she founded the Macondo Foundation and lives in San Antonio, Texas.
literary_profile: Bad Boys (1980, chapbook); The House on Mango Street (1984); Woman Hollering Creek and Other Stories (1991); Loose Woman (1994); Hairs/Pelitos (1994); Caramelo (2002); and A House of My Own: Stories from My Life (2015).
stylistic_characteristics: Short lyrical paragraphs that function as stories; child narrators with an adult's precision; bilingual texture in the names and places; and a sentence built for the voice rather than the plot, learnt in part from the poetry she was writing.
intellectual_concerns: The Mexican American woman's coming of age in Chicago and San Antonio; the house as a figure of belonging and shame; the border and the two languages; violence against women, as in the title story of Woman Hollering Creek; and the pleasures and costs of a woman's independence.
historical_significance: The House on Mango Street is one of the most widely taught books in American secondary and university education and the work through which Cisneros became, with Anzaldúa and Ana Castillo, the best-known Chicana writer of her generation; Woman Hollering Creek is a standard collection of the 1990s. The Norton prints its title story.
bibliographical_notes: The book list, the Arte Público and Random House dates and the Macondo Foundation are from the Wikipedia article checked against the Poetry Foundation author page; the chapbook is listed from its 1980 printing.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Anishinaabe (Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa); novelist, poet and short-story writer writing in English
literary_identity: Anishinaabe novelist whose Love Medicine opened the 1980s Native American novel to a mass readership and whose career has been built on a single interlinked body of fiction
biography: Karen Louise Erdrich was born on 7 June 1954 in Little Falls, Minnesota, and grew up in Wahpeton, North Dakota, where her parents taught at the Bureau of Indian Affairs boarding school; she is an enrolled member of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa. She took a BA from Dartmouth College in 1976, where she met Michael Dorris, and an MA from Johns Hopkins; she worked as a construction worker, a lifeguard and a poetry editor before publishing Jacklight (1984), a book of poems, and Love Medicine (Holt, Rinehart and Winston, 1984), which won the National Book Critics Circle Award. The Beet Queen (1986), Tracks (1988) and The Bingo Palace (1994) extended the same fictional territory around the Argus and Little No Horse families, and The Antelope Wife (1998) began a second, looser series. She won the National Book Award for The Round House in 2012 and the Pulitzer Prize for The Night Watchman in 2021, and she has run Birchbark Books, an independent bookstore in Minneapolis, since 2001. Her sister Heid E. Erdrich is also a poet, and her daughter Aza Erdrich is a writer.
literary_profile: Jacklight (1984); Love Medicine (1984, expanded 1993); The Beet Queen (1986); Tracks (1988); The Bingo Palace (1994); Tales of Burning Love (1996); The Antelope Wife (1998); The Master Butchers Singing Club (2003); The Plague of Doves (2008); The Round House (2012); LaRose (2016); The Night Watchman (2021); and the poetry collections from Jacklight to Little Big Bully (2020).
stylistic_characteristics: Multiple narrators whose accounts overlap and contradict; non-chronological structures that require the reader to assemble the history; a comic and grotesque register inside domestic realism; and a prose that keeps the cadences of Anishinaabe storytelling in English.
intellectual_concerns: Anishinaabe family and community history across the twentieth century; the land, allotment and the loss of a homeland; Catholicism and traditional spirituality held in the same household; violence against Native women; and survival as a comic as well as a tragic fact.
historical_significance: Love Medicine won the National Book Critics Circle Award and is the book generally credited, with Silko's Ceremony and Welch's Winter in the Blood, with opening the Native American Renaissance to a national readership; the linked novels that followed make her the most sustained builder of a fictional world in contemporary Native American writing, and the 2012 National Book Award and 2021 Pulitzer confirmed her standing. 'Fleur' is the chapter through which the Norton represents her.
bibliographical_notes: The novel list, the awards and the biographical facts come from the Wikipedia article checked against the Poetry Foundation author page; the two editions of Love Medicine (1984 and the expanded 1993 version) are distinguished where the record relies on one of them.

birthplace: Jakarta, Indonesia; raised in the United States
nationality_or_literary_tradition: Chinese American (born in Indonesia to Chinese parents); poet writing in English
literary_identity: Chinese American poet of memory, exile and the father, whose first two books made him one of the most admired lyric poets of the 1980s and 1990s
biography: Li-Young Lee was born on 17 August 1957 in Jakarta, Indonesia, the son of Richard Kuan Lee, who had been a personal physician to Mao Zedong before being imprisoned for a year and then exiled, and Joan Yuan Lee. The family fled through Hong Kong, Macau and Japan before reaching the United States in 1964, and Lee grew up in Pennsylvania, where his father became a Presbyterian minister. He studied at the University of Pittsburgh, the University of Arizona and the State University of New York at Brockport, and worked at manual jobs before Rose (BOA Editions, 1986) won the Delmore Schwartz Memorial Award and drew wide attention. The City in Which I Love You (BOA, 1990) was the Lamont Poetry Selection of the Academy of American Poets, and The Winged Seed: A Remembrance (1995) is a prose memoir of his family's exile. Book of My Nights (2001) followed after a long silence, then Behind My Eyes (2008) and The Undressing (2018). He has taught widely and is a distributor of Taoist thought as well as a poet.
literary_profile: Rose (1986); The City in Which I Love You (1990); The Winged Seed: A Remembrance (1995); Book of My Nights (2001); Behind My Eyes (2008); and The Undressing (2018).
stylistic_characteristics: Short unpunctuated free-verse lines with a strong image at the centre; a syntax built on accumulation rather than argument; the sensory detail of food, hands and household objects; and a tone of tender address to a father, a wife or a child.
intellectual_concerns: Exile and the inherited memory of a life before America; the father as a figure of authority, suffering and love; food and eating as acts of intimacy and grief; and the ordinary sacredness of domestic life.
historical_significance: Rose and The City in Which I Love You made Lee one of the most widely anthologised American poets of his generation, and 'Persimmons' and 'The Gift' are standard anthology pieces taught in secondary schools and universities; the Norton prints five poems from Rose, which is a larger representation than most poets of his generation receive.
bibliographical_notes: The collections, the prizes and the family biography are from the Wikipedia article checked against the Poetry Foundation author page and the BOA Editions' author notes; Rose's contents were checked against its table of contents for the five printed poems.

birthplace: Glens Falls, New York, United States
nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; short-story writer and novelist writing in English
literary_identity: American writer of comic and grieving short stories whose wordplay and formal invention made her one of the most imitated story writers of the 1980s and 1990s
biography: Lorrie Moore was born Marie Lorena Moore on 13 January 1957 in Glens Falls, New York, and grew up in the town that appears in her fiction; she won a Seventeen magazine short-story contest at nineteen. She took a BA from St Lawrence University and an MFA from Cornell University, where she studied with Alison Lurie, and worked briefly as a paralegal in Manhattan before teaching. Self-Help (Alfred A. Knopf, 1985) - stories written in the second person and in the form of instructions - made her reputation, and Anagrams (1986), a novel about a woman who rearranges her life through wordplay, extended it. Like Life (1990) and Who Will Run the Frog Hospital? (1994) were followed by Birds of America (Knopf, 1998), which won the Irish Times International Fiction Prize and contains 'People Like That Are the Only People Here', written after her son's cancer. A Gate at the Stairs (2009) and Bark (2014) came later, along with the children's book The Helper (2008). She has taught at the University of Wisconsin-Madison since 1984.
literary_profile: Self-Help (1985); Anagrams (1986); Like Life (1990); Who Will Run the Frog Hospital? (1994); Birds of America (1998); A Gate at the Stairs (2009); and Bark (2014).
stylistic_characteristics: Second-person address and instructional forms used as narrative devices; puns and wordplay that carry grief; a comic timing learnt from stand-up and from the sitcom; and a sentence that is funny in syntax and bleak in content.
intellectual_concerns: Illness and the medical institution, above all in the story the Norton prints; the comedy of ordinary disappointment; women's lives and work; and the way language both protects and fails the person using it.
historical_significance: 'People Like That Are the Only People Here' is one of the most discussed American short stories of the 1990s and is regularly taught as an example of the comic treatment of trauma; Birds of America consolidated Moore's reputation, and the story's inclusion in the Norton is the anthology's principal selection of her work.
bibliographical_notes: The book list and the 1998 Irish Times prize are from the Wikipedia article checked against the Poetry Foundation author page; the story's first appearance in The New Yorker in 1997 is recorded from the magazine's archive and the collection's acknowledgements.
